translations.text: A sermon by our holy father John Chrysostom on Lazarus, who had been dead for four days.
Today Lazarus, rising from the dead, gives us release from great and varied anger.
For I do not know how this reading has brought harm to those of other beliefs and given the Jews grounds for dispute—not because of the truth, certainly not,
but because of the wickedness of their souls. For many of those of other beliefs say
that the Son is not equal to the Father. Why? Because Christ needed prayer to raise Lazarus.
For if he had not prayed, he would not have raised the dead man. How then, they say, is the one who prayed equal to the one who received the prayer?
For the former prayed, while the latter received the prayer from the one praying. But they stumble because they do not understand
that this was an act of condescension, and that the prayer was offered because of the weakness of those present. But tell me, then, who is greater:
the one washing another's feet, or the one whose feet are being washed? Clearly, the greater is the one
whose feet the lesser has washed. Yet the Savior washed the feet of Judas, who betrayed him.
For he was with the disciples. What then? Will you say that Judas, who betrayed him, is greater than Christ,
because Christ washed his feet? Certainly not. And which is more lowly:
to wash feet or to pray? Clearly, washing feet is more lowly
than praying. So if he did not refuse to do the more lowly thing, how could he have refused to do the higher thing?
But all this happened because of the weakness of those present. And that it happened because of the weakness of those present,
the Jews, the sermon will show as it proceeds. But the Jews too, taking this as grounds for dispute, say:
How can Christians regard this man as God, when he did not even know the place?
For the Savior said to Martha and Mary, the sisters of Lazarus: Where have you laid him? Do you see, they say, his ignorance?
Do you see his weakness? This God did not even know the place! But he spoke to them not because this was so,
but because he wished to put them to shame in return. Will you say that Christ did not know the place because he said: Where have you laid him?
Then neither did the Father know, as he walked through paradise, walked through paradise as though looking for
him and saying: Adam, where are you? Where have you hidden? Why did he not name the former place
where Adam used to speak freely with God? Adam, where are you? And what did he answer?
I heard your voice as you walked in paradise, and I was afraid because I am naked, and I hid. If you call this ignorance, then call that ignorance too.
Christ said to Martha and Mary: Where have you laid him? Do you call this ignorance?
For what will you say when you hear God saying to Cain, “Where is Abel your brother?”
If you call this ignorance, then call that ignorance too. Take another example from Holy Scripture.
God said to Abraham, “[?] The outcry of Sodom and Gomorrah has reached me. When I have gone down,
then I will see whether their deeds correspond to the outcry that has reached me; otherwise, I will know.” Yet he knows everything before it comes into being.
God, who examines the kidneys and hearts and kidneys, who alone knows human thoughts, says, “I will go down, then, and see
whether their deeds correspond to the outcry that has reached me; otherwise, I will know.”
If that is ignorance, then this too is ignorance.
But then the Father did not know in the Old Testament, just as the Son did not know in the New Testament. What, then, does this mean: “I will go down, then, and see
whether their deeds correspond to the outcry that has reached me; otherwise, I will know”?
“A report,” he says, “has reached me, but I want to investigate more carefully, testing the deeds themselves.
Not because I do not know, but because I want to teach people not simply to listen to words,
nor to believe someone if he says something against another, but first to investigate these things, and, having learned through examining the deeds themselves,
only then to believe.” That is why he also said in another passage of Scripture, “Do not believe every word.”
For nothing so corrupts human life
as readily believing what is said. The prophet David also proclaimed this, saying, “The one who secretly slandered his neighbor—
him I drove away. With one whose eyes were proud and whose heart was insatiable,
I did not eat.” Do you see that it was not ignorance for the Savior to say, “Where have you laid him?” Just as it was not ignorance for the Father to say, “Where are you, Adam?”
or to Cain, “Where is Abel your brother?” or, “I will go down and see
whether their deeds correspond to the outcry that has reached me; otherwise, I will know.”
Now, then, it is time to take up the fight against those who say that Christ prayed and raised Lazarus because of weakness.
It is not so. Listen with the utmost care, I beg you. Lazarus died,
and Jesus was not in that region, but in Galilee. He said to his disciples, “Lazarus our friend has fallen asleep.”
But they, thinking that he was speaking about ordinary sleep, said to him, “Lord,
if he has fallen asleep, he will recover.” Jesus told them plainly, “Lazarus has died.”
And he came to Jerusalem, to the place where Lazarus lay, and Lazarus’s sister met him.
And she said to him, “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.” The woman spoke in weakness, not knowing
that even without having come, Christ was there by the power of his divinity, but judging by his bodily coming
the Teacher’s power, she said to him, “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.”
“Even now,” she said, “I know that whatever you ask of the Father, he will give you.” So the Savior offers a prayer in response to her request.
For God did not need prayer to raise the dead man. Tell me, did he not raise other dead people?
When he met a dead man being carried out through the gates, did he not merely touch the bier and raise the dead man?
Tell me, did he need prayer then to raise the man who had died? And again, on another occasion,
did he not merely speak a word over the girl, “Talitha koumi,” and give her back to her parents in good health?
Tell me, did he need to pray then? And why do I speak of the Teacher?
His disciples raised the dead with a word. Did not Peter raise Tabitha with a word?
Did not Paul perform many signs through his own garments? And learn something more wonderful: the apostles’ shadow raised the dead.
For they brought the sick on beds so that at least Peter’s shadow might fall on one of them.
And immediately they got up. The disciples’ shadow raised the dead.
But did the Teacher need prayer to raise the dead man? No, he does this because of the woman’s weakness.
For she said to him, “If you had been here, my brother would not have died. Even now,” she said, “I know
that whatever you ask of the Father, the Father will give you.” You ask for prayer; I give prayer.
A spring is there: if someone brings a vessel, it fills the vessel.
If it is large, it will receive much; if it is small, it will receive little. She asked for prayer, and he gave prayer.
And another said, “Speak a word, and my servant will be healed.”
He said to him, “Let it be done for you according to your faith.” Another said, “I am not worthy for you to come under my roof.”
And he said to him, “Let it be done for you as you wish.” Another said, “Come and heal my daughter.”
And he said to him, “I am coming after you.” According to people’s capacity and understanding,
healing is provided by the physician. Another woman secretly touched the hem of his garment,
and she too received healing. Each received healing according to their faith. This woman speaks according to what she knows:
“Whatever you ask of the Father, the Father will give you.” Since she asks for prayer, he gives prayer.
He did not need prayer himself, but accommodated the woman's weakness, and wished to show that he was not opposed to God.
Rather, whatever he does, the Father does also. God fashioned man in the beginning.
The fashioning was the work of both. For [?] made man in our likeness and image.
Again, he wished to bring the robber into paradise. He merely spoke a word and brought the robber into paradise, and had no need of prayer.
Although God had barred everyone after Adam from that entrance.
For he placed a flaming spear to guard paradise. But Christ opened paradise by his authority and brought the robber in.
A robber, Lord? Your Father drove Adam out of paradise for a single sin.
And are you bringing in a robber who, of countless evils and countless transgressions,
is guilty? Thus he brought him into paradise with a single utterance. No, no! That did not happen without me,
nor did this happen without my Father. For this is my work, and that is the Father's. For I am in the Father, and the Father is in me.
And so that you may see that raising the dead man was not the work of prayer, listen to the prayer. What did he say?
“I thank you, Father, that you have heard me.” What had he said? Nothing to the Father before these words.
Yet he said, “You have heard me.” He had said nothing before this utterance, yet he says, “You have heard me.”
Is this a form of prayer? Is this a sign of supplication? “I thank you that you have heard me.”
“But I know,” he said, “that you always hear me.” Then why trouble yourself over things you know?
“But I said this for the sake of this crowd standing around, so that they may understand that you sent me.”
Do you think he prayed for the dead man's sake? Do you think he said, “Father, command Lazarus to rise”?
Do you think he said, “Father, command death to obey me”? Do you think he said, “Command that [?] shut the gates, but quickly give up the dead man”?
“But I said this for the sake of this crowd standing around, so that everyone may understand that you sent me.”
This was by no means the miracle itself, but a proclamation to those who had come. Do you see how the prayer was not for the dead man's sake,
but for the sake of the unbelievers who had come? “So that they may understand,” he said, “that you sent me.” How, then, am I to understand
his saying, “You sent me”? Listen, I beg you, with the utmost care.
“See,” he said, “I call the dead man by my own sovereign power. See, I command death by my own authority.
I call the Father ‘Father,’ so that, if the Father is not my Father,
he may prevent the dead man's resurrection. If the Father is not my Father.”
He makes death surrender the dead man. I call the Father Father.
I also call Lazarus out of the tomb. If the first is not true, then neither will this happen.
But if the Father is truly Father, let the dead man obey [?] those who have come running.
What, then, did Christ say? “Lazarus, come out!” When the prayer was offered, the dead man did not rise.
But when he said, “Lazarus, come out,” then the dead man rose. Oh, the torment of death!
Oh, the torment of that power holding the soul! A prayer was offered; will you still not release the dead man?
“No,” it said. “Why?” “Because I have not been commanded.” There was a certain jailer there, holding the prisoner.
“Unless I am commanded,” he said, “I will not release him. For the prayer,” he said, “was not offered for my sake,
but for the sake of the unbelievers who have come. I have yet to be commanded [?]. I will not release the dead man.
I await Life, so that I may release the soul.” “Lazarus, come out!” The dead man heard the command
and broke the laws of death. Let those of another faith be ashamed! For the word showed that it was not
for the sake of raising the dead man that the prayer was offered, but because of the weakness of the unbelievers who had come there.
“Lazarus, come out!” Why, then, did he call him by name? So that, by letting his voice spread among the dead,
he would not raise everyone in the tombs. For this reason he said, “Lazarus, come out! You alone I call out to now,
so that I may show my power to those passing by. For when I rise in Hades, I will raise the whole world.
For I am the resurrection and the life. Lazarus, come out!”
And the dead man came out, bound in burial cloths. Oh, what great and wondrous miracles!
He who freed the soul from the bonds of death, who threw open the gates of Hades
and shattered the iron doors, and released the soul from the bonds of death—could he not also untie the burial cloths
with which they themselves had bound him when burying him? This was so that through their own bindings they might recognize what they knew,
so that through examination they might accept what they had done: that this is Lazarus, whom they buried,
and that this is Christ, who came by the Father's good pleasure, who has authority over life and death.
To him be glory with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
